lines: A flow simulation has a speed limit. Break it, and the run blows up.
The limit has a name: the Courant number.
Here is a simple test. A block of dye is carried along a pipe. The solver moves it step by step. The edges get soft, but all is well.
Now make the time step three times longer, to save computer time.
Small wiggles appear. They grow at every step, and soon the numbers are huge.
The physics did not change. Only the time step did.
A solver cuts the pipe into cells. Each cell has a width, delta x, and holds one number.
It also cuts time into steps of length delta t. Between two steps, it sees nothing.
The flow has a speed, u. So in one step, the fluid travels a distance of u times delta t.
Compare that distance with the width of a cell. The ratio is the Courant number, C.
It counts how many cells the fluid crosses in one time step.
Half a cell gives one half. A full cell gives one. And a long time step gives two, or more.
Why does this number matter? Look at how a cell gets its new value. The dye obeys the transport equation: it moves with the flow.
The solver replaces each slope with a difference. In time, new minus old. In space, the cell minus its upstream neighbour.
Solve for the new value. And there it is: u delta t over delta x, the Courant number.
Collect the terms. The new value is a mix: one minus C of the cell itself, plus C of its neighbour.
Between zero and one, both weights are positive. The new value lies between the two old ones, so nothing can grow.
At exactly one, the cell takes the value of its neighbour. The dye moves one full cell. A perfect step.
Above one, the fluid comes from beyond the neighbour, where this scheme does not look. One weight turns negative, and the new value shoots past both old ones.
Take a small zigzag error: plus one, minus one, plus one. Put it in the formula, with C at one point five.
Each value becomes minus two times what it was. The error flips its sign and doubles.
It doubles at every step. After twenty steps it is a million times larger. That is the blow-up.
So for this scheme, C must stay at or below one. The time step can be at most delta x over u.
Every cell has its own Courant number. Small cells and fast flow make it large, and the worst cell decides for the whole mesh.
Cut the time step until the largest value is below the limit, and the run is stable.
Refine the mesh by two, and the time step must drop by two as well.
Other schemes have other limits. Implicit ones can run above one, but they lose accuracy there. So check this number first.
To sum up. The Courant number is u delta t over delta x: the cells crossed in one step.
The solver mixes each cell with its upstream neighbour.
Above one, a weight turns negative, and errors grow at every step.
Small cells and fast flow set the time step.
